section.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
section.sectionRationale: Having described the surpassing glory of the new covenant, Paul turns to the paradox of how that glory is carried. The gospel is the light of the glory of Christ, the image of God, yet the god of this age blinds unbelieving minds to it. God has placed this treasure in fragile clay jars, so that the surpassing power is shown to be His and not ours. Hard pressed but not crushed, always carrying the death of Jesus so that His life may be revealed, Paul does not lose heart, for a light and momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory, and he fixes his eyes on the unseen and eternal.
section.thesis: The gospel is the light of the glory of Christ, the image of God, hidden only to those the god of this age has blinded; God carries this treasure in fragile jars of clay so the surpassing power is plainly His, and through affliction that reveals the death and life of Jesus He is producing for His people an eternal weight of glory that outweighs every present trouble.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ shining in hearts; the treasure carried in jars of clay through affliction that reveals the life of Jesus; and the eternal weight of glory that fixes the eyes on the unseen.

units.label: The light of the gospel
units.note: the glory of Christ, the image of God

verses.text: Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart.

Instead, we have renounced secret and shameful ways. We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God. On the contrary, by open proclamation of the truth, we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.
The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the {{eikon|image}} of God.
For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

units.label: Treasure in jars of clay
units.note: the power is God's and not ours

verses.text: Now we have this {{thesauros|treasure}} in {{ostrakinos|jars of clay}} to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.
We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair;
persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.
We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.
For we who are alive are always consigned to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal body.
So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.

units.label: The eternal weight of glory
units.note: fix your eyes on the unseen

verses.text: And in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I have spoken,” we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak,
knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence.
All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.
Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.
For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal {{baros|weight}} of glory that is far beyond comparison.
So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.

eikon.gloss: Image, likeness, exact representation. Christ is the image of God, the one in whom the invisible God is truly seen, as Colossians 1:15 also declares. To behold the glory of Christ is to behold the glory of God Himself, for He perfectly represents the Father. This recalls that humanity was made in God's image; Christ is the true image, and in Him that image is restored in His people.

thesauros.gloss: Treasure, a store of great value. The treasure is the gospel of the glory of Christ, the light of the knowledge of God shining in the heart. Its worth is incalculable, yet God entrusts it to weak and mortal messengers. The contrast between priceless treasure and cheap container is the whole point: the value belongs to the gospel and the power to God, never to the vessel.

ostrakinos.gloss: Made of baked clay, earthenware, fragile and easily broken. Paul pictures himself and every gospel minister as a cheap clay pot holding a priceless treasure. Such jars were common, breakable, and disposable, so the surpassing power is plainly seen to be from God and not from the vessel. The very frailty of the messenger displays that the glory belongs to God alone.

baros.gloss: Weight, heaviness, that which is substantial and full of glory. The Hebrew idea of glory carries the sense of weight, and Paul plays on it: present affliction is light and momentary, but it is producing a weight of glory that is eternal and beyond all comparison. The heaviest suffering is featherlight against the surpassing, everlasting glory being prepared for those who belong to Christ.

basic.context: Paul continues to describe his ministry, now with striking honesty about its cost. He preaches Jesus Christ as Lord openly and refuses all deceit, yet many do not believe, because the god of this age has blinded them to the light of the gospel. Paul frankly admits his own frailty: he is a fragile clay jar carrying an infinitely precious treasure, hard pressed and struck down yet never destroyed, because the power at work is God's. He does not lose heart, for his light momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory.
basic.hermeneutics: This is deeply personal writing, but it teaches truth for every believer, not only apostles. The clay jar imagery interprets suffering: weakness is not a contradiction of ministry but the very means by which God's power is displayed. Read verses 7 to 12 as a pattern of dying and rising that marks the whole Christian life, and verses 16 to 18 as the settled perspective that keeps the suffering believer from despair.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ is the eikon, the image, of God, so to see His glory is to see God. The gospel is a thesauros, a treasure, carried in ostrakinos, jars of clay, cheap and breakable earthenware, so the power is God's. And the present affliction produces a baros, a weight, of glory, playing on the Hebrew sense of glory as weight.
basic.typology: Paul echoes the first day of creation, when God said, Let light shine out of darkness; the same God now shines the light of the gospel into dark hearts. The pattern of carrying the death of Jesus so His life is revealed follows the shape of the cross and resurrection, the paradigm into which every believer is drawn.
basic.christ: Christ is the image of God, the content of the gospel, and the Lord whom Paul proclaims. His glory is the light that shines in the heart, seen in His own face. Paul carries the death of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus may be revealed; the cross and resurrection are lived out in the minister. The God who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise His people with Him.
basic.god: God is the one who gives light, both in creation and in the heart, and whose surpassing power is displayed through weak vessels. He is the merciful God who gives the ministry, the God who raises the dead, and the God whose glory is the goal of everything, so that thanksgiving overflows to His glory. Even suffering serves His purpose, producing an eternal weight of glory.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1 records God speaking light out of darkness. Colossians 1 calls Christ the image of the invisible God. Romans 8 says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come. Philippians 3 speaks of knowing Christ in the fellowship of His sufferings.
basic.oneStory: The God who first spoke light into the darkness now shines the light of the glory of Christ into blinded hearts. He carries this treasure in fragile people so that all the glory is His, and He works through suffering and death to reveal the life of Jesus and to prepare an eternal weight of glory. The whole account moves toward resurrection, when God raises His people with Jesus into His presence.

context.literary:
Chapter 4 has a frame and a centre. The frame is the pair of statements 'we do not lose heart' in verses 1 and 16, each introduced by 'therefore.' The first rests on the mercy that gave the ministry, the second on the renewal of the inner self. Between them Paul works through why a ministry so glorious looks so fragile, and the answer is built in three steps: the message is radiant, the messengers are breakable, and the breaking is part of the purpose.

The centre is the run of four contrasts in verses 8 and 9. Each has the shape 'pressed, but not crushed,' and the effect on the ear is of blow after blow, each met by a 'but not.' Two of the pairs rely on word play that survives in the Greek, and the whole catalogue is an example of what Paul says in verse 7: the pot is cracked and the treasure is not lost. A similar list appears in 6:4-10 and in 11:23-27, and the three should be read together as three views of the same life.

The passage also turns on a sequence of verbs for light and sight. Unbelievers cannot see the light, verse 4. God makes light shine in the heart, verse 6. Paul commends himself to every conscience, verse 2, and at the end he fixes his eyes on what is unseen, verse 18. The chapter starts with a veil, the idea carried over from 3:13-18, and ends with eyes trained on the unseen, so that seeing and not seeing become the question the whole chapter is working through. The opening 'therefore' and the closing movement to chapter 5 make this the hinge of the letter's middle section.
context.historical:
Paul's picture of a clay jar came from daily life. Cheap pottery was the ordinary container for water, oil, grain and lamps in every household. It was bought for pennies and discarded when it broke. Yet clay jars were also used for storing things of real worth, such as the deeds Jeremiah was told to seal in an earthenware jar so that they would last, Jeremiah 32:14. The image has both sides, an unimpressive container and a valuable content, and Paul uses both.

The list of hardships was not literary exaggeration. In 11:23-27 he gives the record: repeated imprisonment, lashings, beatings with rods, a stoning, shipwreck, danger from rivers, robbers and false brothers. In 1:8-10 he says that in Asia he felt the sentence of death on himself and despaired of life. The Corinthians, living in a prosperous port city that valued rhetoric and display, had reason to be embarrassed by an apostle with such a history, and some seem to have taken his sufferings as evidence that he was not truly sent by God.

Verse 4 sets the gospel against a spiritual background Paul's readers would have known. The phrase 'the god of this age' belongs to the Jewish two ages scheme, in which the present age is under the sway of evil and the age to come is God's. John 12:31 and Ephesians 2:2 use similar language of a ruler of this world. Verse 6 draws on the creation story that Jewish and Christian readers knew from Genesis, and verse 13 quotes the Greek version of Psalm 116, the form of the Old Testament the Corinthians would have read.
context.canonical:
The passage is full of the Old Testament. The command of verse 6 recalls the first day of creation, Genesis 1:3, and the language of light dawning on those in darkness is found in Isaiah 9:2 and 60:1-2. Verse 13 quotes a psalm of someone brought through affliction and delivered from death, Psalm 116:10, in the Greek form that begins 'I believed, therefore I spoke.' Paul adopts the psalmist as a fellow believer who speaks because he has faith, not because things are easy.

The clay imagery reaches back to the creation of the human being from the dust, Genesis 2:7, and to the prophets' picture of God as potter and his people as clay, Isaiah 64:8 and Jeremiah 18:1-6. The Psalms say that God knows we are dust, Psalm 103:14. In 2 Timothy 2:20-21 Paul speaks again of vessels of clay and of gold, and in Romans 9:21 of the potter's right over the clay.

The pattern of power through weakness is one of the main strands of Paul's letters. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 puts it in the Lord's own words, 'My power is perfected in weakness,' and 13:4 places the pattern in Christ, who was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power. Philippians 3:10-11 states the same longing to know the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings. Romans 8:18 weighs present sufferings against coming glory, and 1 Peter 1:6-7 compares trial to the refining of gold. The chapter thus belongs to a consistent biblical teaching about the shape of the Christian life.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is answering a charge that must have hurt. Some in Corinth thought a true apostle would be impressive, strong and untroubled, and judged Paul's record of suffering as a mark against him. He answers that the weakness is not an embarrassment to be hidden but a design to be understood. If the power at work in him were his own, no one could tell the difference between a clever speaker and the gospel. Because he is plainly a cracked pot, the power can only be God's.

He also wants to protect the Corinthians from two opposite mistakes. One is to be dazzled by performance and to treat the messenger as the message. The other is to be discouraged when faithful servants suffer, and to assume God has withdrawn. The remedy for both is to see the whole of life in the light of the cross and the resurrection together.

And he wants them to keep going. Twice he says he does not lose heart. He is not describing a feeling he never has, since he admits being perplexed and hard pressed, but a settled determination grounded in what he knows is true. The chapter ends with a practical discipline of attention, learning to weigh what can be seen against what cannot, and he offers it to every reader who suffers.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul describes his own sufferings, and they should not be turned into a requirement. The text does not tell believers to seek hardship or to measure faithfulness by how much they suffer. Verses 8 and 9 record what happened to apostles and how God sustained them. They are a witness to God's keeping power, not a ladder to climb.

What is prescribed is the response. Not losing heart, verses 1 and 16, speaking out of faith, verse 13, and fixing one's eyes on the unseen, verse 18, are meant for all who follow Christ. The pattern of dying and rising in verses 10 to 12 is a description of what happens when a believer's life is lived for others, and Paul says that it is 'for Jesus' sake,' not for its own sake.

A further care is needed with verse 12. 'Death is at work in us, but life is at work in you' describes how apostolic suffering produced life in the churches, and it should not be read as a licence for leaders to cause pain to those they serve or for congregations to demand that leaders suffer. The passage has the generous suffering of an apostle in mind, not suffering that is imposed. Nor is it a promise that every hardship produces a visible benefit. It gives the believer a settled hope that nothing suffered for Christ is wasted.

debates.question: Who is the god of this age who blinds minds?

views.label: Satan
views.case: The historic reading takes the god of this age as the devil, who blinds unbelievers to keep them from the light of the gospel, consistent with Paul calling him the ruler of this world elsewhere.

views.label: A description of idolatry or self
views.case: A few take it as the spirit of the age or the false gods people serve; but the personal act of blinding fits a personal being, so most affirm the reference to Satan.

debates.bearing: Either way the cause of unbelief is not a defect in the gospel but a spiritual blindness only God can lift by shining light into the heart.

debates.question: Does carrying the death of Jesus refer to Paul alone or to all believers?

views.label: Primarily Paul's apostolic suffering
views.case: The immediate reference is to Paul and his fellow workers, whose afflictions display the life of Jesus to the churches.

views.label: A pattern for every believer
views.case: The dying and rising shape of the Christian life applies to all who are united to Christ, as Romans 8 and Philippians 3 confirm, so the passage instructs every sufferer.

debates.bearing: The primary reference is apostolic, yet the pattern is paradigmatic, so all believers may take comfort that weakness and suffering are the arena of God's resurrection power.

debates.question: Does the inner self of verse 16 mean the soul as something separate from the body?

views.label: A soul that outlasts the body
views.case: Some read the inner self as the immortal part of a person, so that as the body wastes away the soul is renewed. They point to chapter 5, where Paul speaks of being away from the body and at home with the Lord, and to the sense of unseen realities in verse 18.

views.label: The whole person renewed by God
views.case: Others note that Paul uses the phrase of the person seen from the side of God's work, as in Ephesians 3:16, and that he hopes for a resurrection body, 5:1-4, so he is not setting a good soul against a bad body. The contrast is between what is passing and what is being made new.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that renewal is God's present work in the believer and that it will be completed in resurrection. The verse should not be used to teach that the body does not matter, since the very next chapter shows Paul longing for it to be clothed with immortality, not discarded.

study.originalLanguages:
The two pairs in verse 8 that end in 'despair' play on words in Greek. Aporoumenoi means 'at a loss,' and exaporoumenoi means 'completely at a loss.' Paul is saying something like 'at a loss, but not utterly lost.' The English 'perplexed, but not in despair' keeps the idea without the sound. The first pair uses stenochoreo, which has the sense of being squeezed into a narrow space, and its negative describes room to move. Each of the four pairs therefore describes pressure that stops short of the final blow: hemmed in but not shut in, at a loss but not lost, pursued but not abandoned, thrown down but not destroyed.

In verse 10 the word translated 'death' is not thanatos, the usual word, but nekrosis. It means a putting to death, or a state of deadness, and the only other place the word appears in the New Testament is Romans 4:19, where Abraham considers the deadness of Sarah's womb. The word fits the context: what Paul carries in his body is the dying process of Jesus, and it is in just such deadness that God has historically brought life. The verb for carrying about, peripherontes, suggests being carried around in a public way, like someone who is on show.

In verse 11 the phrase 'consigned to death' translates paradidometha, 'we are handed over.' It is the verb used of Jesus being delivered up in Romans 4:25 and 8:32. Paul's experience of being given over has the form of the Lord's own, and the passive is the passive of God's purpose as well as of human opposition.

Verse 16 contrasts the 'outer self,' ho exo anthropos, with the 'inner self,' ho eso anthropos. The second expression appears in Romans 7:22 and Ephesians 3:16. It is not a Greek idea of an immortal soul trapped in a body, because Paul goes on to long for a resurrection body in chapter 5. The inner self is the person as God renews them. The verb 'is being renewed' is anakainoutai, a present passive, which signals continued action from outside. The phrase 'day by day' is literally 'day and day.'

Two more words repay attention. In verse 17 the affliction is 'light' (elaphron) and 'momentary' (parautika, for the present moment), while the glory is a weight and, literally, 'according to excess into excess,' kath' huperbolen eis huperbolen. The same noun 'surpassing' appeared in verse 7 for the power, so the same kind of excess is found at both ends of the passage: the power that carries us and the glory that awaits us. Finally, 'fix our eyes' translates skopeo, to look attentively at a mark or goal. It is used for fixing attention on an example in Philippians 3:17. The unseen things are described as proskaira for what is seen, meaning only for a season, as against aionia, eternal.

typology.type: The first creation of light, Genesis 1:3
typology.fulfillment: On the first day God spoke into a formless dark and there was light. Paul says the same God has spoken again, but this time into the darkness of the human heart, giving the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The link is that new creation follows the pattern of the first, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The escalation is that the light in the heart is the glory of God seen in a person. The type does not mean the first creation was a symbol only, but it does show that salvation is a work of creative power, not persuasion.

typology.type: Humanity as clay in the potter's hands, Isaiah 64:8 and Jeremiah 18:1-6
typology.fulfillment: In the prophets Israel is clay and God is the potter, and the vessel can be reshaped. Paul takes the picture of clay and makes it a description of the apostles. The clay is ordinary, breakable and made to be used, and what it holds is the treasure of the gospel. In Christ the potter does not merely reshape his vessels; he places inside them the light of his own glory. The picture falls short if pressed: clay vessels do not suffer, and Paul's point is that real human beings share the Lord's own dying and rising.

Gideon's three hundred men carried a torch inside a jar, and when they broke the jars the light flashed out and the enemy was thrown into confusion. Paul does not cite this story, so it should be treated as a possible echo, not a claim of the text. If it is heard at all, it makes a fitting parallel: the light shines when the container is broken, and the victory belongs to the LORD. The correspondence is only suggestive, and the passage stands without it.

typology.type: The pattern of death and resurrection, John 12:24
typology.fulfillment: Jesus said that a grain of wheat remains alone unless it falls into the ground and dies, and that if it dies it bears much fruit. Paul's phrase 'death is at work in us, but life is at work in you,' verse 12, has the same shape. The life of Christ is released through his death, and the lives of his servants become fruitful as they are given up. The fulfilment is not that believers repeat the atonement, which Christ finished once for all, but that they share the form of his path, Philippians 3:10.

study.christ:
Christ stands at the centre of this chapter in three roles: he is the content of the gospel, the image of God and the pattern of the believer's path. Paul says that he does not proclaim himself but 'Jesus Christ as Lord,' verse 5, and everything else in the chapter depends on that sentence.

He is the image of God, verse 4. The word eikon means a likeness that shows what the original is. Colossians 1:15 says the same, that the Son is the image of the invisible God, and it adds that all things were created in him. This explains why the gospel is called 'the gospel of the glory of Christ.' To see the glory of Christ is to see what God is like, and verse 6 says it is 'in the face of Jesus Christ' that the knowledge of the glory of God is given. The first Adam was made in the image of God and defaced it. Christ is the true image, and he has come to restore it.

He is the pattern for the minister. The death of Jesus is carried in the body, verse 10, and the life of Jesus is revealed in the same body. This is not a loose comparison. The path from the cross to the empty tomb is the shape of the apostle's life. Paul says in 13:4 that Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God, and that believers are weak in him and will live with him by that power. In this way Christ is not only the one preached but also the one whose pattern the preacher embodies.

He is also the one who raises. Verse 14 says that God, who raised the Lord Jesus, will raise us with Jesus. The resurrection of Christ is the guarantee and the pattern of the believer's, and the phrase 'with Jesus' means that the destiny of his people is bound to his. Romans 8:11 makes the same link through the Spirit. This is why Paul can speak of present death and still say he does not lose heart.

Christ is the light that dispels the blindness. The god of this age blinds, and God commands light to shine. The conflict in verses 4 to 6 is not just between competing ideas but between two powers, and what overcomes the blindness is a revelation of Christ himself. The pattern of Paul's own conversion, in which a light from heaven struck him on the road to Damascus, Acts 9:3 and 26:13-15, gives this language personal force.

A caution applies. The jar of clay is not itself a picture of Christ, who was not a flawed vessel. The point of correspondence is in the pattern of weakness and power, not in a comparison of material. And Paul is careful to say that the death of Jesus is 'carried' and its life 'revealed.' He does not say that the believer adds to what Christ has done, only that he shares in it and lets it show.
study.god:
This chapter shows God in several lights, and the first is as the giver of light. In verse 6 God speaks and the light shines, and what he does in the heart repeats what he did at the creation. This means conversion is not something people achieve by being clever or good. It is an act of the Creator, which is why Paul can say the blinding of unbelievers is overcome only by God's word.

God is merciful. The ministry itself is something he gave 'in His mercy,' verse 1, and the word shows that Paul sees no merit in himself. The man who once persecuted the church has been given the task of preaching it, and he does not forget that it was a gift. Mercy lies behind the ministry, and mercy lies behind the believer's survival.

God is the one who is sovereign over weakness. He has chosen to put his treasure in clay, and verse 7 gives the reason: so that the surpassing power is shown to be from God and not from us. This is a deliberate arrangement. It runs against the instinct that God's work is best done with impressive instruments, and it fits the pattern of Israel's story, in which God repeatedly worked through the small, the barren and the overlooked, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29. The God of the Bible takes pleasure in showing his strength where no one can mistake the source.

He is faithful in suffering. The four contrasts of verses 8 and 9 are not claims about Paul's resilience but about God's keeping. Paul is not abandoned, because the one who holds him does not let go. Romans 8:35-39 lists a similar series of troubles and ends with the certainty that none can separate us from the love of Christ. God does not remove the pressure, but he sets a limit to it.

He is the God who raises the dead, verse 14. That title is also used in 1:9 and Romans 4:17, and it describes God's character as much as his power. Because he raises the dead, nothing that happens to those who trust him is final. He is also the God who is glorified in thanksgiving, verse 15. The goal of the grace spreading through the world is that more and more people will give thanks, and so the purpose of all of this is the worship of God.

For worship, this chapter teaches that praise is not limited to happy circumstances. A person who is hard pressed and perplexed can still thank God, because the grounds for thanksgiving do not lie in circumstances. God's light has shone, his power is at work and his glory is to come. Faith in such a God is expressed in speaking, verse 13, and in thanking.

crossReferences.note: God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light. Paul's wording in verse 6 is his own summary and not an exact quotation, but the point is plain. The God who commanded light on the first day is the God who now shines in the heart, so that new birth is described as a new creation.

The psalm that Paul quotes in verse 13. The speaker is a person afflicted and nearly killed who believes and therefore speaks. Paul uses it to say that his preaching, in the midst of suffering, comes from the same spirit of faith, and that those who believe will be delivered as the psalmist was.

The Son is the image of the invisible God. It matches the statement of 4:4 and adds that all things were created in him. Together the two verses explain why seeing the glory of Christ is seeing the glory of God, and why the gospel of his glory is the only true light.

The Lord's answer to Paul's prayer: his grace is sufficient and his power is perfected in weakness. It supplies the divine word behind the picture of the clay jar, and explains why Paul can boast in weaknesses and delight in hardships for the sake of Christ.

The record of what Paul means by being hard pressed and struck down: imprisonments, beatings, a stoning, shipwrecks and constant danger. Reading the list beside 4:8-9 shows that the contrasts are descriptions of real events and not poetic exaggerations.

Present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed. It is Paul's parallel to the weighing of verse 17, and it shows that the idea of glory outweighing suffering is a considered conviction, not a passing comfort for one hard season.

Paul's wish to know Christ and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to him in his death. It states in a personal way what 2 Corinthians 4:10-12 says about carrying the death of Jesus so that his life may be seen.

Darkness covers the earth, but the glory of the LORD rises on his people. It shows how the prophets spoke of God's light shining in a dark world, and prepares for Paul's claim that this light has now dawned in the face of Christ and shines in the hearts of those who believe.

Deeds sealed and put in a clay jar to be preserved for a long time. It shows that earthenware could be used to protect what mattered most. The detail supports the paradox in verse 7, since a common jar is exactly where something of lasting worth might be kept.

Believers are told to run with endurance, fixing their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. It joins 2 Corinthians 4:18 in teaching that perseverance depends on where we look, and names the one whom the unseen things finally centre on.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with two things that this chapter holds together: light spoken into darkness, and a human being made from the dust. Genesis 1:3 gives the light and Genesis 2:7 gives the clay. After the fall the human vessel is cracked, and the creation story is darkened by sin, so that the whole Old Testament waits for a new word from God. Isaiah promises that a people in darkness will see a great light, Isaiah 9:2, and in Paul's gospel that light has come.

The chapter also continues a pattern that runs through the Scriptures: God works through weak instruments. He chose Abraham and Sarah, who had no child, a Moses slow of speech, a young shepherd David, a remnant of Israel, and finally a baby in a manger and a man on a cross. At every step he took care to make clear that the power was his, as the verse says. The jar of clay is in a long line of such choices, and it explains why the church's message and its messengers so often look fragile.

Looking ahead, the chapter points to resurrection. Verse 14 anchors the believer's hope in the resurrection of Jesus, and 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 says what is sown in weakness is raised in power. The next chapter takes up the same theme, and Paul will say that the earthly tent is taken down and a building from God awaits. The affliction here is not the end of the story, because the story's end is glory.

The new creation is where the pattern finishes. Romans 8:18-21 says that creation itself waits to be set free, and Revelation 21:4 promises that death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more. In that world the treasure will no longer be carried in clay, and the glory that is now seen in a mirror will be seen face to face, 1 Corinthians 13:12. What the faithful carry in weakness will then be worn in splendour, and God will be seen to have done what he said: light out of darkness, life out of death.

quiz.q: Why do some people fail to see the light of the gospel?

options.text: The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers to the glory of Christ.
options.note: Verse 4 locates the problem in spiritual blindness, not a flaw in the gospel.

options.text: The gospel itself is unclear and poorly explained.
options.note: Paul proclaims the truth openly; the veil is on the hearer, not the message.

options.text: God has not chosen to save anyone at all.
options.note: God does shine light in hearts; the blinding is the work of the god of this age.

options.text: They are simply not intelligent enough to understand.
options.note: The issue is spiritual blindness, not intelligence.

quiz.q: Why does God place the treasure of the gospel in jars of clay?

options.text: So that the surpassing power is shown to be from God and not from us.
options.note: Verse 7 states the reason plainly: the power belongs to God.

options.text: Because God could not find any stronger vessels.
options.note: God chooses weak vessels on purpose, not by necessity.

options.text: To keep the gospel hidden from most people.
options.note: The point is displaying God's power, not concealing the gospel.

options.text: Because human strength is what makes ministry succeed.
options.note: The opposite is true; weakness displays that the power is God's.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by always carrying around the death of Jesus?

options.text: His sufferings share the pattern of the cross so the risen life of Jesus is revealed in him.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 tie dying with Christ to the revealing of His life.

options.text: He constantly feels guilty about the crucifixion.
options.note: It is union with Christ's death, not lingering guilt.

options.text: He literally re-enacts the crucifixion in worship.
options.note: Paul speaks of real affliction, not a ritual re-enactment.

options.text: He expects to be crucified exactly as Jesus was.
options.note: He means the general pattern of suffering and life, not identical death.

quiz.q: How does Paul keep from losing heart in affliction?

options.text: He fixes his eyes on the unseen and eternal, knowing affliction produces an eternal weight of glory.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18 give the settled perspective that outweighs present trouble.

options.text: He tells himself his troubles are not really happening.
options.note: Paul does not deny the affliction; he weighs it against eternal glory.

options.text: He expects God to remove every hardship immediately.
options.note: He endures affliction rather than expecting its instant removal.

options.text: He relies on his own inner strength to press on.
options.note: His hope rests on God who raises the dead, not on self reliance.

questions: Paul admits he is a fragile clay jar, yet God's power works through him. How does it free you to serve when you stop needing to be strong or impressive?
The god of this age blinds minds to the gospel. How does knowing that unbelief is spiritual blindness change the way you pray for those who do not yet believe?
Paul is hard pressed but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed. Where do you need to hear that promise in your own pressures right now?
Present affliction is light and momentary compared to an eternal weight of glory. What present trouble looks heavy to you, and how does weighing it against eternity change it?
Paul fixes his eyes on what is unseen and eternal. What seen things tend to dominate your attention, and what would it look like to fix your eyes on the unseen this week?

translationNotes.note: The god of this age is most naturally read as Satan, who blinds the minds of unbelievers; the phrase describes his usurped dominion over the present age, not a rival deity to the one true God.
Some manuscripts read in the face of Christ rather than in the face of Jesus Christ; the meaning is unchanged, that the glory of God is seen in the person of Christ.

The phrase rendered eternal weight of glory plays on baros, weight, and the Hebrew idea that glory is weighty; the light momentary affliction is deliberately set against the surpassing, everlasting weight of glory.
